title: CSS Selectors
subtitle: Target HTML elements using element, class, ID and attribute selectors.
description: Master the selectors CSS uses to decide exactly which elements should receive a particular style.

blocks.text: Welcome to Lesson 2: CSS Selectors. This lesson follows the course dashboard topic “CSS Selectors”. The goal is to target HTML elements using element, class, ID and attribute selectors.. Focus on understanding when this technique is useful, what assumptions it makes, and how you can check that it is working.

Selectors tell CSS which elements should receive declarations. Element selectors apply broadly, class selectors are reusable, and ID selectors are intended for a unique element; attribute and pseudo-class selectors can target more specific states.

blocks.question: A card style should apply to many cards, not just one unique element. Which selector is usually reusable?
options: An ID selector reused for every card.
A selector based on the card’s current text.
A universal selector for all page elements.
blocks.explanation: Classes can be applied consistently to many components; IDs should be unique in a document.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Classes can be applied consistently to many components; IDs should be unique in a document.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Classes can be applied consistently to many components; IDs should be unique in a document.

blocks.question: A hover rule is not taking effect because another rule wins. What is the best debugging step?
options: Add ten copies of the hover rule.
Inspect the cascade and specificity of the competing declarations.
blocks.explanation: Inspecting computed styles reveals which declarations win and why.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Inspecting computed styles reveals which declarations win and why.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Inspecting computed styles reveals which declarations win and why.

blocks.text: When two declarations compete, the cascade considers importance, origin, specificity, and source order. A selector that is too specific can make later maintenance harder, so prefer reusable classes and clear component boundaries.

blocks.question: A selector must target a required input. Which selector is appropriate?
blocks.explanation: An attribute selector can target inputs whose required attribute is present.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. An attribute selector can target inputs whose required attribute is present.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. An attribute selector can target inputs whose required attribute is present.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Apply it and check your reasoning
Debug by inspecting the element and checking which rule wins rather than adding random overrides. A smaller, predictable stylesheet is usually easier to maintain than a large chain of exceptions.

options: Use OR if either rule must pass.
Skip validation once the page looks correct.
Combine both checks with the appropriate AND condition.
